articles.title: Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP
articles.summary: Josh Babarinde's proposal is also supported by other MPs, including David Lammy and Sir James Cleverly.
articles.body:
The next census should include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English, according to a group of MPs.

Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde told the BBC that "most people" in the country believe "you don't have to be white to be English", as he called for the categories to be updated in a similar way to changes in Wales and Scotland.

At the 2021 census, the ethnic group section saw English offered only within the white category.

Babarinde's proposal, dubbed the "St George's Bill", aims to broaden the options and its supporters include Labour's David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly. It was tabled in the House of Commons on Tuesday.

In his speech to introduce his private member's bill (PMB), Babarinde told MPs he is a "proud Englishman" and has "proud Nigerian heritage".

He said: "But my parents and I were born in England, we grew up in England, our home is in England, yet some voices attempt to reduce Englishness to a skin colour and to a bloodline.

"Well, if we're going to go down that path, my mum's side of the family has been English for as far back as we have traced."

The Eastbourne MP said he had received "death threats for daring to say that you don't have to be white to be English".

He added "English ethnicity is real" before arguing it is a "matter of historical fact that it has never been one bloodline" and "even our Royal Family has German roots".

"Is the King not English either, I ask."

Addressing the ethnicity section of the census, Babarinde said the "only box that says English sits under the white category".

He added: "If you are black, the form offers you black British, if you are Asian, it offers you Asian British, but not English.

"Now, the same question in the Welsh census offers a black Welsh category. In Scotland, the census offers Scottish Asian, for example.

"Yet the best that England offers in our census is a miscellaneous write-in box that may as well be the margin."

Lammy, a former deputy prime minister, said in a statement: "It is quite absurd that neither I or my mixed heritage children can describe themselves as black or mixed race and English on our census form.

"I have long campaigned for us to change to the position enjoyed by others in Wales and Scotland. We have to end this backward racial gatekeeping."

Babarinde told the BBC he had brought forward the PMB because there were "some corners of our politics who are attempting to gatekeep Englishness for people who are a particular colour".

He also said there are "people like Suella Braverman who have really undermined and questioned the Englishness of people like me".

In 2025, Braverman - then a Conservative MP before her defection to Reform UK - wrote in the Daily Telegraph that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.

In recent weeks, Braverman has reaffirmed her position and wrote on X : "To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage."

She also said "Englishness is an ethnicity", adding: "There have been English people for centuries and we need to recognise this more if we are to start taking a more muscular approach to citizenship and nationality. And no, it's not racist to say this."

Babarinde introduced his PMB to the Commons using the 10-minute rule process.

This gave him up to 10 minutes to make the case for why he wanted to introduce his PMB.

No MP took up the option to make a 10-minute speech opposing it.

Babarinde asked for his PMB, formally known as the English Ethnic Identity (census particulars) Bill, to return to the Commons on 23 April 2027 - St George's Day - for its second reading debate.

But it is unlikely to be considered further in its current form due to a lack of parliamentary time.

PMBs allow MPs to raise issues they believe ministers should be considering and to develop campaigns showing the strength of support for their ideas.

articles.title: Hawaii Supreme Court to hear whether two elephants held at Honolulu Zoo for decades can challenge their captivity through habeas corpus; conservation group seeks their release to a sanctuary
articles.summary: Two Asian elephants that have spent decades at the Honolulu Zoo are at the centre of a legal battle that could reshape how courts consider the rights of
articles.body: Two Asian elephants that have spent decades at the Honolulu Zoo are at the centre of a legal battle that could reshape how courts consider the rights of animals. The Hawaii Supreme Court is examining whether Mari and Vaigai can use habeas corpus, a legal remedy traditionally associated with challenging unlawful human detention, to contest their confinement. The Nonhuman Rights Project (NhRP), which is seeking their transfer to an accredited sanctuary, argues that the elephants deserve protection for their fundamental interest in bodily liberty. The case has drawn attention to animal welfare, legal personhood and the limits of existing laws.Hawaii Supreme Court is hearing the elephant captivity caseAccording to the Nonhuman Rights Project, the Hawaii Supreme Court agreed in June 2026 to hear the case after the organisation challenged earlier rulings against its petition. The court granted an application for a writ of certiorari, allowing it to review the lower court decision and consider the legal questions raised by Mari and Vaigai's confinement.A November 9 hearing was subsequently scheduled, as reported by the organisation. The proceedings concern whether the elephants can bring a habeas corpus claim and whether their captivity can be challenged through that legal mechanism.The case, known as Nonhuman Rights Project v. C&C of Honolulu, et al., follows a petition originally filed in 2023. The NhRP sought to have the elephants moved from the zoo to an accredited sanctuary, arguing that their needs and abilities warrant a different form of legal protection.The organisation's application reached the Supreme Court after Hawaii's Intermediate Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal of the petition in January 2026. The NhRP then filed for review in April, according to its court update.Mari and Vaigai have lived at the zoo for decadesMari was captured in the wild and brought to the Honolulu Zoo in 1982, while Vaigai arrived in 1992, the Nonhuman Rights Project states. Both are wild-born Asian elephants who have spent much of their lives in captivity.The Florida Bar Animal Law Section describes the elephants as living in a habitat measuring approximately 68,244 square feet. It contrasts that space with the extensive ranges Asian elephants can occupy in the wild, which may span several square miles.Asian elephants may travel up to 10 miles in a day and occupy home ranges extending to roughly 500 square miles.The NhRP argues that the enclosure cannot accommodate the animals' complex physical, social and behavioural needs. Its legal position rests on the claim that elephants possess advanced cognitive abilities, emotional lives and enduring social relationships, making freedom to direct their lives an important interest.What does habeas corpus mean for elephantsHabeas corpus is a legal process through which a court examines whether someone is being unlawfully detained and should be freed. The NhRP wants Hawaii's courts to consider whether the same protection can apply to elephants, rather than limiting it exclusively to humans.As per Civil Beat, the case should not be reduced to a demand for human rights for animals. The petition seeks a specific protection, bodily liberty, rather than every right recognised for people.The argument is that legal systems can recognise limited protections for entities without treating them as human. Civil Beat cited corporate free speech protections as an example of how legal safeguards may extend beyond human beings without granting them an entire set of human rights.The NhRP maintains that the elephants' advanced abilities and interest in autonomy should be recognised in law. The organisation says scientific evidence submitted in the case describes elephants as capable of problem-solving, forming lifelong bonds, experiencing grief and displaying complex emotions.Why the case has divided animal rights advocates and criticsThe legal challenge has attracted support from animal law advocates as well as criticism from groups concerned about the wider implications of recognising legal rights for animals.The Hawaii Animal Law Section filed a supporting brief, according to the Florida Bar Animal Law Section. It argued that the case could be considered in light of Hawaii's Aloha Spirit, a cultural principle associated with kindness, unity, humility and respect for nature.The section also pointed to Hawaii's legal framework, which permits courts to consider the Aloha Spirit when making decisions. It believes the principle supports a more compassionate approach to the elephants' confinement.The NSSF, however, presents a contrasting perspective. It warned that extending habeas corpus to elephants could have consequences beyond zoo captivity, potentially opening the door to legal challenges involving animal ownership, livestock and wildlife management.The organisation stressed that animal welfare protections and legal personhood are separate issues. It also cited the zoo's position that Mari and Vaigai receive veterinary attention, enrichment and opportunities to walk within their habitat.The sanctuary proposal remains central to the disputeThe NhRP is not seeking to release Mari and Vaigai into the wild. Its petition proposes transferring them to an accredited sanctuary where they could have greater space and opportunities to express natural behaviours.The sanctuary proposal was an effort to address the elephants' needs without necessarily granting them the full range of rights enjoyed by humans.The debate also reflects Hawaii's history with captive elephants. The Florida Bar Animal Law Section recalled the 1994 incident involving Tyke, an elephant who escaped from a travelling circus in Honolulu, killed one person and injured others before being fatally shot. The incident led Hawaii to prohibit the importation of animals for exhibition.The earlier appellate ruling found that the relevant statute applied to human persons and did not extend the remedy to elephants. The outcome could influence future debates about how courts recognise the interests of cognitively advanced animals.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Renaissance landscape bought by a Swiss collector in 1957 vanished from public view for nearly 70 years; experts have identified it as a rare Altdorfer worth up to £5 million
articles.summary: A small Renaissance painting that remained in a private Swiss collection for nearly seven decades is set to make its way into the international art
articles.body: A small Renaissance painting that remained in a private Swiss collection for nearly seven decades is set to make its way into the international art market, with an estimated value of up to £5 million. The work, attributed to German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer, is particularly significant because it could become the third known oil landscape by the artist, whose surviving works of this kind are exceptionally rare. According to The Guardian, The Art Newspaper and Sotheby's, the painting dates to around 1520 and will be offered at Sotheby's Old Masters Evening Sale in London on December 9, 2026. It carries an estimate of £3 million to £5 million and is being presented as a previously unknown work that has emerged from a Swiss private collection. Measuring just 23.4 by 19.8 centimetres, the painting depicts a densely wooded landscape, with a rainbow appearing behind the trees, a distant rocky outcrop and a sky filled with heavy clouds. Despite its modest dimensions, the artwork is considered an important addition to the known body of work of the Northern Renaissance artist.A painting with an unusual place in art historyThe work, titled A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky, is signed with Altdorfer's monogram on the trunk of a tree. Sotheby's catalogue describes it as an oil painting on parchment, which was later attached to a wooden panel.Its significance lies in the way it treats nature as the central subject rather than using a landscape merely as a background for human figures or a religious story. Altdorfer was among the early European artists to explore landscape painting as an independent genre, giving forests, weather and natural scenery a prominent place in his work.Until this painting came to light, only two comparable oil landscapes by the artist were widely recognised. One, Landscape With a Footbridge, is part of London's National Gallery collection, while the other, Landscape of the Danube near Regensburg, is housed at Munich's Alte Pinakothek. The newly identified painting would expand that small group to three.From an Austrian aristocratic collection to SwitzerlandThe painting's documented ownership history goes back to the collection of the House of Harrach, an Austrian aristocratic family that once kept it at the Palais Harrach in Vienna. It was purchased in 1957 by the father of the current owner and remained in the family after the acquisition. Its appearance at Sotheby's marks its return to public attention after decades away from museum displays and the international art market.The discovery is also significant because Altdorfer paintings rarely become available to collectors. The last time a work by the artist entered the market was in 1980, when the National Gallery acquired Christ Taking Leave of His Mother, another painting dating to around 1520, for a reported £2.45 million. The acquisition was considered one of the most expensive art purchases of its time.Who was Albrecht Altdorfer?Born in Regensburg, in present-day Bavaria, Albrecht Altdorfer became one of the leading figures of the German Renaissance. He initially established himself through drawings and engravings before developing an interest in painting natural scenery in the early 16th century.His landscapes drew inspiration from the forests and river valleys around the Danube. He also received important royal commissions, including The Battle of Alexander at Issus, completed in 1529 for Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria. The monumental painting is now held at the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. Altdorfer spent much of his career in Regensburg, where he also held public office, and died there in 1538. His approach to depicting nature helped establish landscape painting as an important artistic subject in its own right.Where the painting will be displayedBefore the December auction, Sotheby's is presenting the painting at its New York exhibition from November 7 to 19, followed by a London viewing from December 4 to 9. The auction house has placed an estimate of £3 million to £5 million on the work, although its eventual selling price remains uncertain. With no comparable Altdorfer painting having appeared on the market for decades, the sale is expected to attract interest from major collectors and museums.For the art world, however, the significance of the discovery extends beyond its potential auction price. A painting that spent almost 70 years outside public view could add a rare new chapter to the understanding of one of the Renaissance's pioneering landscape artists.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Iowa woman co-owned a house bought with a $260,775 mortgage but never signed the loan note; when the lender tried to foreclose without notifying her, the state supreme court reversed the foreclosure ruling
articles.summary: Owning a home jointly does not always mean both owners sign the same loan documents.
articles.body: Owning a home jointly does not always mean both owners sign the same loan documents. But when a lender moves to foreclose on a property, the distinction can become crucial, particularly when one co-owner is not given an opportunity to prevent the foreclosure. In Iowa, a woman who jointly owned and lived in a house but had never signed its promissory note challenged a foreclosure after the lender failed to send her a notice giving her an opportunity to catch up on missed payments.The Iowa Supreme Court ruled in her favour on November 6, 2026, in Newrez LLC, d/b/a Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing v. Lynae D McMillen Dickey Tesdall. The decision, available on Justia, reversed the district court's foreclosure judgment and vacated an earlier appeals court decision. The justices held that the woman qualified as a borrower under the mortgage and was therefore entitled to a separate notice of her right to cure the default before foreclosure proceedings could move forward.Woman co-owned the house but did not sign the loan noteThe dispute began in 2019, when Lynae D McMillen Dickey Tesdall and Donald S Aegerter purchased a house in Mason City, Iowa, as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. Wells Fargo Bank provided $260,775 in secured financing for the purchase. Although both were listed as borrowers on the mortgage document, only Aegerter signed the promissory note. Tesdall did not sign the note and was not personally responsible for repaying the loan.However, the mortgage identified both individuals as borrowers and required them to make payments when due. It also clarified that someone who signed the mortgage but not the note was not personally obligated to repay the secured debt. The distinction became important when their circumstances changed. Aegerter moved out of the house in November 2021 and relocated to Waterloo, while Tesdall continued living at the Mason City property.In June 2022, the mortgage went into default. Wells Fargo subsequently sent notices of the right to cure to Aegerter at both the Mason City property and his new address in Waterloo. No notice was sent to Tesdall.Lender refused to provide her with loan informationBetween July and December 2022, Tesdall repeatedly attempted to contact Wells Fargo to obtain information about the outstanding payments. However, representatives reportedly refused to provide her with details, saying they were not authorised to do so. The notice sent to Aegerter in August 2022 stated that the overdue amount was $6,110.54. Tesdall maintained that she could have arranged sufficient funds to clear the overdue payments if she had received the same notice and been given the opportunity.In February 2023, Wells Fargo filed a foreclosure lawsuit against both co-owners. The bank argued that payments had not been made since May 2022 and sought to foreclose on the property. The amount claimed, including principal, interest and fees, exceeded $247,000. Tesdall challenged the action, arguing that she had not received the legally required notice of her right to cure the default.In August 2024, while the foreclosure case was pending, Wells Fargo assigned the mortgage to Newrez LLC, doing business as Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing, which was then substituted as the plaintiff. The district court nevertheless granted summary judgment in favour of the lender. It reasoned that Tesdall was not entitled to the notice because she had not signed the promissory note and was not personally liable for repayment. It also relied on a mortgage provision stating that notice to one borrower would count as notice to all borrowers. The Iowa Court of Appeals upheld that decision, prompting Tesdall to seek further review before the state Supreme Court.Why the Iowa Supreme Court reversed the foreclosure rulingThe Supreme Court examined Iowa Code Section 654.2D, which requires lenders seeking to foreclose on a homestead to provide borrowers with a notice of the right to cure a default. The law gives borrowers 30 days from the date the creditor gives the notice to pay overdue instalments or otherwise correct the default before the creditor can proceed with foreclosure.The justices disagreed with the lower courts' interpretation of the term borrower. They explained that the relevant question was whether Tesdall was a borrower on the mortgage, not whether she had personally signed the underlying promissory note. The court pointed out that Wells Fargo's own mortgage document identified her as a borrower. She also owned 50% of the property, lived there and had pledged her ownership interest as security for the financing. The justices further explained that Iowa's homestead laws are intended to protect homeowners and must be interpreted broadly in their favour.They rejected the lender's argument that notifying one borrower was sufficient. Under the applicable law, each borrower entitled to protection had to receive the required notice. The court also noted that Aegerter no longer lived at the property, while Tesdall continued to occupy it as her home.Case sent back for further proceedingsThe Supreme Court concluded that Tesdall was a borrower under the mortgage and was entitled to receive a notice of her right to cure the default. It reversed the district court's judgment, vacated the Court of Appeals' decision and remanded the case for further proceedings. The justices left it to the lower court on remand to consider whether the statutory requirement to prove substantial prejudice applies when a lender fails to provide a notice altogether, rather than providing a notice with defects. Her affidavit stated that she could have obtained enough money to clear the overdue amount if she had been notified.The ruling does not permanently prevent foreclosure or erase the outstanding mortgage debt. Instead, it establishes that a co-owner identified as a borrower on a mortgage cannot be denied statutory homestead protections simply because they did not sign the promissory note.You use AI every day. articles.title: 80% of Delhi's pollution Monday due to crackers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Firecracker emissions accounted for more than 80% of Delhi's pollution load on Monday, a day after Diwali, according to the Indian Institute of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Firecracker emissions accounted for more than 80% of Delhi's pollution load on Monday, a day after Diwali, according to the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology's models, highlighting the sharp impact of fireworks on the capital's air quality. The contribution came even as the city was already battling high pollution levels from multiple sources.The situation, however, showed some improvement on Tuesday, with the AQI at 299 at 4pm, bringing it into the 'poor' category from 'very poor' a day earlier. However, it deteriorated to very poor by 6pm with an AQI of 302.Toxins from Diwali firecrackers lingered on Tuesday as well, with IITM showing 29.9% of pollution contribution due to firecrackers between 1am and 9am, while secondary organic compounds - formed due to chemical reactions of emitted particles in air - were the secondary source at 17.5% of net pollution on Tuesday. IMD attributed cleaner air to favourable wind, which helped disperse pollutants accumulated over the city and barred intrusion of stubble smoke from neighbouring states.Vehicular emissions third biggest source of pollution day after DiwaliThe easing came despite a significant number of farm fires being reported in neighbouring Punjab. An assessment of the decision support system for air quality management indicated that stubble burning was not a major contributor to Delhi’s pollution load on Monday. This suggests that the immediate post-Diwali pollution spike was driven primarily by local fireworks rather than a major influx of crop-residue smoke.The high contribution from firecrackers followed a sharp deterioration in air quality during the festival. Delhi’s average AQI was 376 on Diwali, Nov 8, the highest recorded for the festival in five years. It remained in the ‘very poor’ category on Monday, with the city waking up to a thick layer of smog and several monitoring stations reporting severe air quality.IITM’s model estimates the contribution of different sources to the city’s particulate pollution a day after Diwali on Nov 9, including secondary organic compounds, at 5.8%, the second dominant source, and vehicular pollution at 4.4%, the third biggest source. However, the city’s air quality will depend on how effectively winds disperse the remaining pollutants and on emissions from routine sources.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Anger and frustration as Newport medieval ship set to remain in storage
articles.summary: Campaigners want a permanent home for the 15th Century trading ship, which was discovered in 2002.
articles.body:
Campaigners say they are "angry and frustrated" that a medieval ship discovered in Newport nearly 25 years ago is still no closer to being given a permanent home.

The 15th Century Newport Ship was found in 2002 in the muddy riverbank of the Usk during construction of the Riverfront Theatre in the city centre.

But councillors are expected to confirm the ship will continue to be kept in storage for the foreseeable future, given the estimated £27.5m cost of building a permanent display venue.

Another factor is the "very limited availability" of a suitable site in Newport, although the council says its long-term ambition is "to enhance public interpretation of the ship".

After being found, the ship's timbers were disassembled and went through an extensive restoration process before the 2,500 parts were finally returned to a storage facility in Newport.

The site is occasionally open to visitors, though campaigners' long-term ambition is to see it restored and reassembled to its full 30m (98.4 ft) size, in a similar manner to the Tudor-era Mary Rose warship in Portsmouth.

"She's a wonderful find from the time of the great voyages of exploration, where Europe reached out to the other continents," said Charles Ferris, chair of Friends of the Newport Ship.

"It's like somebody finding, say, the Space Shuttle in 600 years' time.

"She's not a warship, she's a trader and that's a wonderful thing to me because that's the heart of Newport."

But a new report, set to be considered by Newport City Council's cabinet on Wednesday, has recommended keeping the existing storage arrangements that currently cost £115,000 a year.

Options outlined include a trial reassembly project, or a permanent display facility, but the council noted that "no ready-made facility exists" and that such a site would cost around £27.5m.

Transferring the ship to a custodian outside of Newport for display and preservation was also "something the council is not looking to do".

"While the council's long-term ambition remains to enhance public interpretation of the ship, there is no proposal at the moment that is fully developed, funded and capable of delivery within a sustainable operating model," the report added.

Ship could be Wales' answer to the Mary Rose

But that has infuriated opposition councillors, who say a permanent display for the ship would boost tourism.

"We've been talking about this for a decade now," said Matthew Evans, who leads the council's Conservative group.

"I'm very disappointed at the lack of action, the lack of ambition.

"We're talking about a world-class opportunity here for tourism.

"The Mary Rose has hundreds of thousands of visitors, and we've just sat on our backsides and done nothing at all, kicked it into long grass.

"I'm angry and frustrated at the lack of progress."

Evans acknowledged the council could not be expected to fund the entire project, but rejected claims there were no suitable locations in Newport.

"We've got plenty of sites along the riverfront we could have been talking to developers about, but we haven't done it," he said.

"You find a site, then you look at private investors, and then you build that from there.

"The council needs to be driving this – I'm tired of all these excuses, no action."

Successive council administrations have shown a "lack of ambition" in making the most of the "fantastic resource" that was discovered, says one of the area's Senedd members.

"There's an opportunity there to, in conjunction with the Transporter Bridge and maybe Caerleon, [for] a package of historical tourism, if you like," said Plaid Cymru MS Peredur Owen Griffiths.

"For the city, it could well be an excellent way of looking at how to invest in new facilities for the ship.

"And I think I'm a little bit disappointed in Newport council that their ambition is to put this into further storage for another few years, rather than look at the opportunities that might be available."

Campaigners are also anxious to see the ship remain in Newport, rather than being displayed at a museum facility elsewhere in the future.

"A lot of money has been spent on that ship, so we're really on the last stretch as it were, we don't want to see it fizzle out now," said Ferris.

"I think it would be a tragedy if it was ever taken anywhere else. That would be a terrible indictment on us, and after all it was the will of the Newport people that saved it."

articles.title: A Tennessee family won back access after a neighbour fenced off half their shared driveway; when they sued the city over the fence permit, a federal judge ruled the permit did not amount to a government taking
articles.summary: A Tennessee family has regained access to a shared driveway after a neighbour built a fence through it, blocking their use of part of the driveway.
articles.body: A Tennessee family has regained access to a shared driveway after a neighbour built a fence through it, blocking their use of part of the driveway. However, their separate lawsuit against the city that approved the fence permit has ended in a defeat, with a federal judge ruling that issuing the permit did not amount to a government taking of their property.According to the ruling, Mark McDonald, Nanette McDonald and their daughter Madeleine McDonald own a property in the City of Oak Hill in Davidson County, Tennessee. Their daughter lives in the house, which was built in 1965. The neighbouring property belonged to Mary Rust, whose house was built in the 1950s.Both properties had used a common driveway since the houses were built. The arrangement was based on reciprocal easements, which allowed the owners of each property to use the portion of the driveway located on the neighbouring land.The dispute began after Rust sought to make improvements to her property. According to the family's complaint, she learnt that the city's rules for calculating plot sizes excluded land covered by an easement. This meant she could not make certain improvements while the driveway easement remained in place.Rust asked the McDonalds to sign an agreement ending the easement, but they refused. She then approached the city in July 2024 to enquire about building a fence along the property boundary, which ran through the middle of the shared driveway.Neighbour builds fence after obtaining city permitA city code enforcement officer told Rust that she needed a building permit to construct the fence. The city's zoning rules also required applicants to submit a site plan showing the property's boundaries, easements and other details. The family said the city also required a stamped survey showing property lines and easements.Initially, the code enforcement officer told Rust that she could not get permission to build the fence through the driveway if the portion on her property was covered by an easement.However, Rust later submitted a Deed of Correction signed by the previous owners of her property. The document, dated October 29, 2024, stated that a joint driveway agreement recorded in 1992 was not an easement and was not intended to remain binding on future owners.Rust told the city that the document had removed references to the easement from her deed and effectively ended the arrangement.According to the McDonalds, the city attorney accepted this explanation and concluded that the document was sufficient to remove the easement. The family maintained that the city knew they disagreed and continued to assert their rights over the driveway.Despite the dispute, the city approved Rust's application and issued a building permit on November 21, 2024. Rust then constructed the fence down the middle of the driveway, preventing the family from using the portion covered by their easement.The McDonalds maintained that the easement could not be ended without their consent. They also argued that the 1992 agreement had created a valid property right that continued to apply even after the neighbouring property changed hands.Family wins driveway dispute against neighbourThe family first challenged the fence through legal action against Rust. On December 6, 2024, they filed a case in the Davidson County Chancery Court.They sought a declaration confirming their rights over the driveway, along with damages for defamation of title, interference with the easement and trespass.They also appealed the city's decision to issue the building permit before the Board of Zoning Appeals. However, the board said it did not have the expertise or authority to decide disputes over private property rights.In September 2025, the family and Rust reached an agreed order in the state court case. The order confirmed the validity of the driveway easement, nullified the Deed of Correction and required Rust to remove the fence.This restored the family's legal access to the portion of the driveway on Rust's property. The two sides later settled the family's claims for damages in June 2026.However, the family continued its legal fight against the City of Oak Hill. They argued that the city's decision to approve the fence permit had effectively taken away their property rights.Federal judge rejects family's claim against cityThe McDonalds filed a separate lawsuit against the city, arguing that issuing the permit amounted to an unlawful taking under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the US Constitution.They also accused the city of failing to train its code enforcement officials properly and of following a policy that favoured issuing permits over protecting existing property rights.The family argued that the city should have refused the permit until the dispute over the easement was resolved. They said allowing Rust to build the fence had deprived them of access to a property right they legally held.The city disputed the claim. It argued that issuing a building permit did not amount to a decision on who owned the disputed property or whether the easement was valid.In a memorandum filed on November 5, US District Judge Aleta A Trauger agreed with the city. The judge acknowledged that the family had a valid property interest in the driveway easement when the permit was issued. However, she said the key question was whether the city's decision to grant the permit itself amounted to a taking.The court found that it did not. It said the permit only authorised Rust to build a fence and did not establish that she had the legal right to build it on land covered by the family's easement.The judge said the city had not attempted to settle the property dispute or terminate the easement through the permit. Instead, Rust's decision to construct the fence had interfered with the family's property rights.The memorandum stated that Rust's actions, rather than the city's issuance of the building permit, had caused the family's loss of access.The judge also explained that a building permit does not give a person the right to construct something on another person's property without obtaining the necessary permission.Even if the city had been negligent in issuing the permit before the easement dispute was settled, that alone did not establish a constitutional violation, the court said.The judge therefore granted the city's motion for judgment on the pleadings and rejected the family's request for partial judgment. The court dismissed the case in its entirety.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Sting says his six children will not inherit his multimillion-dollar fortune; explains why he believes giving them too much money would be harmful
articles.summary: British musician Sting has reiterated that his six children will not inherit a substantial fortune from him, arguing that giving them too much money could
articles.body: British musician Sting has reiterated that his six children will not inherit a substantial fortune from him, arguing that giving them too much money could do more harm than good. The singer, whose real name is Gordon Matthew Thomas Sumner, believes children should develop independence and learn to build their own lives rather than rely on inherited wealth. In a recent interview, the Police frontman explained why he considers financial responsibility and a strong work ethic more valuable than leaving behind a large inheritance. His position, first made public more than a decade ago, remains unchanged.Why Sting believes his six children should not inherit his fortuneSting reaffirmed his inheritance plans during an interview with CBS News Sunday Morning in May 2026. The musician laughed when the subject of his children's inheritance came up but remained firm about his position.He explained that giving children enough money to avoid working could undermine their motivation and independence. Sting described the prospect of removing the need for work from a child's life as a form of abuse, reflecting his belief that employment and personal achievement are important parts of growing up.The singer's reasoning is not simply about limiting access to money. It is rooted in the idea that children should develop the confidence to support themselves and make their own decisions without depending on their parents' financial resources.As Entertainment Weekly reported, Sting believes his children have already developed the work ethic necessary to succeed independently, making a substantial inheritance unnecessary.How does Sting define financial support for his childrenWhile Sting does not intend to leave his children a large inheritance, he has made clear that this does not mean refusing to support them altogether.During the CBS interview, he explained that he has paid for their education and provided for their basic needs. His approach is to ensure they have the foundations to build their own lives without removing the responsibility of earning a living.Global News reported that Sting described his children's independence as something he respects. When asked whether they ever became frustrated with his financial philosophy, he said they did not express such feelings directly to him.He also stressed that his position was not intended to be harsh. Instead, he sees it as an expression of confidence in his children's abilities and a belief that they can manage their own futures.The singer has indicated that he would step in if any of his children faced genuine financial difficulties. However, he said he had rarely needed to do so because they were motivated to succeed through their own efforts.Sting's concerns about trust funds and inherited wealthSting's views on inheritance date back to at least 2014, when he discussed the subject in an interview with the Mail on Sunday, as reported by CBS News.At the time, he said he did not want to leave trust funds that could become burdens for his children. He also explained that his family had considerable financial commitments and that much of the money coming in was being spent.CBS News reported that Sting's wealth was estimated at £180 million, equivalent to around US$306 million.Who are Sting's six childrenSting has six adult children from two marriages, as detailed by Entertainment Weekly. His family includes children who have pursued careers in music, acting and other creative fields.His first marriage was to actress Frances Tomelty, which lasted from 1976 to 1984. The couple had two children, son Joe Sumner and daughter Fuschia Sumner.Sting later married actress and producer Trudie Styler in August 1992. They have four children together: Mickey Sumner, Jake Sumner, Eliot Sumner and Giacomo Sumner.The musician's comments suggest that he sees their individual careers and independence as evidence that his approach to parenting has worked.Why Sting continues to work despite his wealthIn the CBS interview, he explained that he enjoys working and does not particularly want to retire.Entertainment Weekly reported that the singer remains motivated by his profession, despite having accumulated substantial wealth through decades of music and performance. His career includes his time as frontman of The Police and his subsequent success as a solo artist.He believes the experience of working, earning and achieving goals provides something that money alone cannot offer. With all six children now adults, Sting believes they are capable of managing their own lives.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: American Airlines plane nearly hit by Air France jet after takeoff at LAX
articles.summary: Air traffic control audio captured the tense moment an Air France jet made an unauthorized turn into the path of an American Airlines flight at LAX recently. An expert weighed in.
articles.body: Two passenger jets operated by Air France and American Airlines came dangerously close in the air after departing from Los Angeles International Airport recently. The incident happened at about 12:20 a.m. on Nov. 7 after the Air France aircraft made a turn it had not been cleared to make, according to a statement the Federal Aviation Administration provided to Fox News Digital. articles.title: Stickers and building sets help drive toy sales ahead of Christmas rush
articles.summary: A bumper year so far for toy sales comes as debate intensifies over screen time and tech connectivity.
articles.body:
Traditional games and stickers are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.

The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.

The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.

The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10.

Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".

The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.

This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.

Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular.

"Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices.

A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.

Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day .

One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family.

Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play.

"Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said.

The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year.

It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg.

Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs.

There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said.

Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe.

articles.title: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns
articles.summary: The Office for Students says students can frequently use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected".
articles.body:
Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said.

The Office for Students (OfS) said "a significant proportion" of assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed to a high standard with AI, sometimes in minutes.

It said this posed a "significant risk" to their credibility, and closed-book and practical exams were the most effective forms of assessments.

Universities UK said many institutions had "made substantial changes" to make assessments "AI-proof".

Universities that do not meet OfS quality standards could soon be banned from charging increased tuition fees or have caps imposed on their student numbers, under proposals that are now being consulted on.

The new research from the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that gives awards for teaching excellence, is based on the views of 244 higher education staff and 91 students from at least 127 universities.

It said "a significant proportion of assessments" were in "unsupervised, non-controlled formats where AI can be accessed by students completing them".

"Many of these can be completed to a high standard using AI tools with limited engagement from students," it added.

It also concluded it was "frequently possible" for students to use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected".

Unsupervised assessment can include coursework, but also remote online exams. They were rolled out widely during Covid, and research from Swansea University last year suggests 93 universities in the UK still use them in some form.

Josh Fleming, director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said there were "fantastic" examples of universities seizing opportunities presented by AI, but there should be "far greater use of AI-free assessment".

"It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them," he said.

Kathryn Harrison-Graves, deputy chief executive at Advance HE, said students wanted "greater clarity about what is expected of them" but staff had "varying levels of confidence and support".

Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up

'Misleading' student loans information left out examples of higher-salary repayments

The OfS said it had heard of cases where students were completing entire assessments within minutes using AI and receiving similar grades to those who had not.

Some staff, meanwhile, were receiving lots of assignments that looked the same, and did not think their institution's assessments were "fit for purpose".

Other staff described a "polarised atmosphere" between students who used AI and other "conscientious objectors" who avoided it on environmental and other grounds.

The research said AI literacy for students was important during and after university, and some institutions were clearly communicating to students where AI can and cannot be used in assessments.

But it said there was "an urgent need" to ensure that remote or "non-secure" assessments "maintain their validity despite the availability of AI tools, meaning they effectively assess the knowledge and skills they are designed to measure".

"If it becomes possible to complete an assessment using AI without the knowledge and skills being tested, the assessment should be replaced," it added.

Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, said universities were "making significant progress" adapting to AI.

"There is further to go but many have made substantial changes to how they assess students. This includes more in-person exams, presentations, vivas, process-based assessment and assessments that integrate AI in a controlled way," a spokesperson said.

"Different subjects will require different approaches, and universities should have the flexibility to adopt assessment methods that best support learning outcomes."

Lewis Wilson, from the National Union of Students, said AI was threatening "traditional" ways of learning that students and staff "have long said is not fit for purpose" - including essay questions, handouts and slideshows.

"It's time to get rid of the outdated methods, that have been kept around in the name of tradition, and instead encourage the innovative practice we see across the sector, co-designed with students based on what they want from higher education," he said.

articles.title: A Queensland mother was ordered to pay to transport her son's modular home to an island after a family court battle involving a pet macaw, a pool robot and household belongings
articles.summary: A Queensland mother has been ordered to pay for the transportation of her son's $24,000 modular home to Russell Island following a family court battle
articles.body: A Queensland mother has been ordered to pay for the transportation of her son's $24,000 modular home to Russell Island following a family court battle involving a pet macaw, a pool-cleaning robot and disputed household belongings. The District Court of Queensland ruled that Aaron Spencer was entitled to possession of the home, which had been moved to his mother's property in Tamborine. His mother, Charlene Martin, must arrange for a third-party truck to deliver the structure and cover the transport costs. The ruling also ordered her to pay $14,306.65 in damages and a further $1,326.40 in interest.What happened after the Queensland family court ordered the property to be vacatedAccording to the Court Judgement, the dispute originated at a residential property in Moggill, Queensland, which Martin and her husband, Peter Spencer, jointly owned. Following the breakdown of their marriage, the couple became involved in family law proceedings in late 2020. Martin had moved out of the property, while their son continued living there. The Family Court subsequently appointed Martin as trustee for the sale of the property and ordered Peter Spencer to vacate it within 42 days of an order made on 14 May 2024.The order also authorised the issue of a warrant of possession if the property was not vacated within the required period. A warrant was eventually issued on 19 September 2024 and executed on 23 September. Aaron Spencer was given limited time to collect his personal belongings and left with several bags containing designer clothing, electronic devices, car keys and confidential paperwork, as well as his three dogs. A pet macaw named Smurf remained at the property. The court noted that a police officer had told Spencer he could return later with an appropriate truck to collect his property.Why did the Queensland family dispute extend to a pool robot and modular homeFollowing the execution of the warrant, Martin took possession of the property and began preparing it for sale. An email sent by her solicitors on 24 September 2024 stated that she was packing household belongings into a shipping container for later collection. The correspondence also addressed the pet bird left behind, stating that Martin was taking care of it until her son could collect it. The email explained: "She is taking care of the bird until such time as the son can collect it."The dispute over Smurf was subsequently resolved separately. On 15 May 2026, the court made final orders by consent concerning ownership and possession of the macaw, an indoor parrot cage, a stand and an outdoor aviary. The judgment did not examine those matters further. The remaining proceedings concerned ownership and the alleged wrongful retention or disposal of various belongings, including glass fencing, a custom-built door, a pool robot, household items, food and the modular container home. The court examined the evidence provided by both parties, including invoices, receipts, photographs, videos and witness testimony.Why did the judge reject some of Spencer's ownership claimsJudge Dann considered whether Spencer had established ownership and an immediate right to possession of the individual items he claimed. The judgment noted that he had relied on a combination of purchase invoices, sales dockets and other supporting material. However, the court also identified inconsistencies in some of his evidence, particularly concerning Costco purchases, where multiple membership and payment card details appeared on the documents. The judge was not satisfied that the available records established that Spencer had purchased every item he claimed.Nevertheless, the court accepted his ownership claims for several belongings supported by independent evidence. These included glass fencing, a custom-built door, a pool robot and food. The judgment recorded that the glass panels had been used to reinstate the pool fence to make the Moggill property compliant for sale. Spencer also accepted Martin's explanation that the pool robot had been left with the house when it was sold. The court found that Martin had disposed of fresh, frozen and dried food, while evidence from Spencer's grandparents established that they regularly sent him food from the United Kingdom.How did the court rule on the son's modular home and household belongingsThe modular container home became a central part of the final orders. Martin's evidence was that the home had been professionally moved to an acreage property in Tamborine, where it remained in her possession. Spencer provided invoices and proof of payment establishing that he had purchased it for $24,000, including GST. The court found there was no evident dispute over his ownership of the structure and ruled that he was entitled to possession.In considering the appropriate remedy, Judge Dann noted that the home was large and heavy and would require professional skills to move. The judgment stated: "The appropriate remedy in this circumstance is to order Ms Martin to pay for the delivery up of the modular container home to Mr Spencer." The final orders required a third-party truck to collect it from 2057-2061 Waterford-Tamborine Road, Tamborine, before or on 1 July 2026, for delivery to Spencer at 55 Fenton Road, Russell Island, on 3 July 2026. Martin was specifically ordered to pay the cost of the truck.In addition to the transport arrangement, Martin was ordered to pay $14,306.65 in damages for the conversion of the glass fencing, custom-built door, pool robot, one set of iron gates and hinges, commercial log splitter, air-conditioning unit and food. The court also awarded $1,326.40 in interest under section 58 of the Civil Proceedings Act 2011. Both amounts were payable by 20 September 2026. The judge dismissed the remainder of Spencer's claim, finding that he had not established his case in relation to the other items he sought to recover.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
articles.summary: But the court dismisses the other part of Trump's lawsuit that alleged the BBC had violated a Florida law.
articles.body:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.

Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit

A judge ordered Trump last month to answer questions under oath in the lawsuit by 11 December, after the president cancelled a previous deposition last month, citing "matters of national importance".

A lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia in October on the scheduled day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Earlier this year, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally argued - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, from his defamation lawsuit, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

articles.title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terrorist attacks, including planned attack against U.K. air base
articles.summary: One of the men helped direct the planned attack against the air base while he was in a U.S. prison, according to a Justice Department indictment.
articles.body: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force. Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City. Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed. “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement. The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England. The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.” The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say. Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody. Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri. In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators. His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said. The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah. In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

articles.title: When senior citizens aided forest dept personnel rescue an injured lesser whistling duck in Chennai
articles.summary: CHENNAI: On Monday evening, as the city started bursting the leftover Diwali firecrackers, a lesser whistling duck hit a multi-storey building in T Nagar
articles.body: CHENNAI: On Monday evening, as the city started bursting the leftover Diwali firecrackers, a lesser whistling duck hit a multi-storey building in T Nagar and fell on the ground. The brown and chestnut-coloured bird lost its flight after a few feathers of a wing were damaged.Someone lifted the bird and tried to make it airborne again. It flew some metres and hit a nearby apartment building. It perched on the sunshade of the first-floor apartment looking at the fireworks-lit sky, perhaps in the direction its flock had flown away. The species is commonly found near lakes and paddy fields in the country, and it flies slowly with rapid wing-flapping and produces whistling while flying.Rescuing the bird from the sunshade was not easy. Someone suggested seeking the help of the forest department.There were not many staffers at the Velachery forest office on Monday night. But two forest staff members came with a cage. They went to the apartment. The purpose was to reach the sunshade from the balcony of the second-floor apartment. But the house was locked.They tried their luck in two neighbouring apartments. Two senior citizens, who opened the doors, initially suspected the strangers. But they became enthused on hearing the purpose of the visit.The occupant on the first floor opened the balcony. One of the forest department personnel tried to reach the sunshade from there. The commotion disturbed the duck, which flew, hit the next building, fell on the ground and again tried to soar, only to hit a nearby villa and fall in the backyard.Rescuing the bird from the villa’s backyard appeared more difficult as the security guard wouldn’t let the forest personnel in. The guard telephoned the house owner. The house owner, a senior citizen, came walking slowly. On learning the purpose, he asked the guard to open the gate of the backyard.The bird resisted rescue, but ultimately it yielded and found itself comfortable in the cage.The bird was bleeding. articles.title: Winnipeg man was charged after allegedly diverting $11,600 from fake fundraiser for teenage crash victim’s funeral; about 240 donors contributed, but the grieving family received nothing
articles.summary: Winnipeg fundraising fraud charges followed a police investigation into a fake online campaign that claimed to help the family of a teenager who died in a
articles.body: Winnipeg fundraising fraud charges followed a police investigation into a fake online campaign that claimed to help the family of a teenager who died in a motor vehicle crash in October 2022. Police allege the donations, given by roughly 240 people, were routed into a personal bank account and none reached the grieving family. A Winnipeg man, 20 when police announced the case, was charged with fraud over $5,000, laundering proceeds of crime and theft over $5,000. The suspect and the victims were not previously known to one another, police said, and the Financial Crimes Unit took over the investigation.How a Winnipeg fundraiser was allegedly set up under fictitious organisers after a teenager’s deathAccording to Winnipeg Police Service, officers investigated the death of 17-year-old David Bunguke in a collision in the St. Vital neighbourhood. In the days after his death, a male suspect allegedly created a campaign on a public fundraising platform, presented as a way to help his grieving family pay for the funeral through donations. Under the guise of fictitious organisers, police allege, the suspect linked his personal bank account as the account that would receive the money.About $11,600 in donations was diverted into the suspect’s own accounts, police allegeThe campaign drew its donors in the space of one week. Between the end of October and early November last year, police allege, the suspect diverted about $11,600 of that money into his own accounts, and it was later used for personal gain. As fraud was suspected, police were contacted.How the suspect turned himself in to police in February 2025 and was released on an undertakingInvestigators identified a suspect believed to be involved and, on 25 February 2025, took him into custody after he turned himself in. He was released on an undertaking, as mandated by the Criminal Code. Police announced the charges on 1 May 2025, and the release reports no court outcome.Platform protections let some donors claim reimbursement, and police ask the public to report fraudProvisions built into the fundraising platform to guard against suspicious campaigns allowed some affected donors to receive reimbursement through claim submissions, police said. Anyone with information about suspected fraudulent online donation activity can report it to their local law enforcement agency and to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.You use AI every day. articles.title: Turning Point USA Spox Andrew Kolvet speaks out as Jennifer Welch, Dave Chappelle mock Charlie Kirk's murder
articles.summary: Andrew Kolvet slams Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan's apology as narcissistic and calls Dave Chappelle's remarks about Charlie Kirk deeply disappointing.
articles.body: Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet is firing back at "I've Had It" podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan and comedian Dave Chappelle for making light of Charlie Kirk's murder in recent days. "We're not asking people to, you know, be evangelical Christians here. We're asking don't celebrate, condone or glorify political violence. Don't be happy when someone's assassinated. It's a very, very low bar," Kolvet told Fox News Digital in an interview. Last week, Welch and Sullivan sparked backlash for laughing uncontrollably while reading an online post that read, "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again" as they celebrated Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms. After several sponsors pulled their ads, Welch and Sullivan issued an apology, though Welch later insisted it wasn't meant for Kolvet or others offended by the mockery, saying the apology "was for us." WELCH DOUBLES DOWN ON TPUSA FEUD, CALLS GROUP 'LOSERS' AFTER LAUGHING AT JOKE ABOUT KILLING CHARLIE KIRK AGAIN "Pro tip, an apology is for the other person," Kolvet reacted to Welch. "It is for people that you've aggrieved and hurt. It's not for you, unless you're a narcissist. And then I guess it is about you. So, that was pretty shocking." Several sponsors have dropped the podcast since Welch and Sullivan's laughing fit went viral over the past several days. Though he said neither he nor TPUSA were behind what he calls the "grassroots" boycott movement against the podcast, he celebrated the decision reached by various companies once associated with the show. "I'm generally not pro-cancel culture, but I also believe that these brands get their own free speech," Kolvet said. "These brands get to have the speech to say, 'I don't want to be associated with somebody that celebrates the murder of an innocent man because of his politics.' CHAPPELLE, JENNIFER WELCH JOKES ABOUT KIRK'S MURDER PART OF PATTERN OF LEFTISTS FINDING HUMOR IN VIOLENCE "I'm not asking for Jennifer Welch to be imprisoned. I'm not asking for her to not have a show or to be able to express her opinions. ... All I'm saying is it's not that hard. Don't celebrate political violence," he continued. "Don't laugh at it. Don't rub it in our faces that one of the most important people in the conservative movement in the country for Gen Z was murdered in cold blood. Don't do it. Don't be a ghoul, don't be vile, don't spew that venom and don't perpetuate that culture. "Cause when you do, you're participating in something very dark and brands, consumers, Americans all have a right to say what they feel about your antics and your behavior," Kolvet added. He said Welch's "apology" ended up doing more harm to her and her podcast than good and rejected her assertion that the boycott movement was TPUSA attempting to wage war on her podcast. "Nobody's done this to you, Jennifer. You've done this to yourself," he told Welch. "I don't expect you to listen to me but maybe, just maybe you will listen to all those brands who no longer want to be associated with you." HOW CHARLIE KIRK’S ASSASSINATION CHANGED THE WAY CONSERVATIVES APPROACH HOSTILE OPPONENTS Despite Welch's "petty" insistence that she would never sit down with him, Kolvet said he would "totally sit down with her." "I wouldn't do it for content. I would sit down in a closed-door space, and my heart would be open, and I would be generous and gracious to her and hope that it would be a fruitful conversation," he said. "My expectation for that is infinitesimally low, but certainly I would be open to that. "You know, Charlie modeled that," Kolvet continued. "He was willing to talk to anybody. He was willing to talk to people that hated his guts. ... But Charlie wanted to have those conversations because he knew that once conversations stopped happening, that's when violence happens. "And, so, our conversation, our debate is an escape hatch," he added. "It's a release valve for the tensions in our culture. And, you know, hopefully she changes her mind and her posture about having conversations with people that don't agree with her completely." Regarding Chappelle, Kolvet said he has no intention to "speech police him" but that what he told a crowd at Madison Square Garden that he "feel[s] better" after Kirk's assassination was "a really crazy thing to say." Kolvet hearkened back to the nation's response to the 1981 assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan, saying he learned from reports at the time that only one obscure comedian cracked a joke about it at a Los Angeles comedy club. He noted that the joke "bombed" and pointed out that the Academy Awards ceremony was delayed by a day out of respect for the recovering president. "Ronald Reagan was not a popular president in the media in 1981. He was much maligned, as a matter of fact, but the country as a whole understood that political assassination is an evil, evil thing," Kolvet said. Kirk defended Chappelle in 2022 after a man attacked the comedian while he was performing at the Hollywood Bowl after controversy over his jokes about transgender people. SOCIAL MEDIA HORRIFIED BY DAVE CHAPPELLE’S SICK ‘JOKE’ ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK’S MURDER "Charlie saw the writing on the wall," Kolvet told Fox News Digital. "Charlie was always warning against the rise of political violence, warning against the rise of assassination culture. And, obviously, it's deeply disappointing that Dave Chappelle couldn't return those sympathies to Charlie when Charlie lost his life. "We need to be kind to our fellow Americans," he continued. "We need to wish the best for them. We need to hope for their safety and that just because I disagree with you politically doesn't mean that I wish ill upon you or physical harm. As a matter of fact, I hope you're safe, and I hope that you live a long life and I hope I can convince you on the merits of my arguments, or you can convince me of yours. "But political violence is not something to be toyed around with, and our culture literally depends on us having a bright line right there," Kolvet said.
